claim: The visual system contextualizes incomplete scene fragments by exploiting spatial schemata.
source: Here we show that the visual system achieves this contextualization by exploiting spatial schemata, that is our knowledge about the composition of natural scenes.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by fMRI and EEG data showing schema-based sorting of scene fragments.

claim: Schema-based sorting of scene fragment representations occurs in the occipital place area (OPA).
source: We observed a sorting of representations according to the fragments' place within the scene schema, which occurred during perceptual analysis in the occipital place area and within the first 200 ms of vision.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data showing vertical location organization in OPA (t[29] = 4.12, p<0.001).

claim: Schema-based sorting occurs within the first 200 ms of vision.
source: We observed a sorting of representations according to the fragments' place within the scene schema, which occurred during perceptual analysis in the occipital place area and within the first 200 ms of vision.
evidence: Supported by EEG data showing vertical location effects from 55 ms to 685 ms with peak around 200 ms.

claim: Schema-based coding operates flexibly across visual features as measured by a deep neural network model.
source: This schema-based coding operates flexibly across visual features (as measured by a deep neural network model) and different types of environments (indoor and outdoor scenes).
evidence: Vertical location information persisted in OPA and EEG after regressing out DNN features.

claim: Schema-based coding operates flexibly across different types of environments (indoor and outdoor scenes).
source: This schema-based coding operates flexibly across visual features (as measured by a deep neural network model) and different types of environments (indoor and outdoor scenes).
evidence: Vertical location predicted cortical organization when restricted to comparisons between indoor and outdoor scenes.

claim: Schemata were first introduced to philosophy by Kant to explain how prior knowledge enables perception of the world.
source: First introduced to philosophy to explain how prior knowledge enables perception of the world (Kant, 1781), schemata were later adapted by psychology (Barlett, 1932; Piaget, 1926) and computer science (Minsky, 1975; Rumelhart, 1980) as a means to formalize mechanisms enabling natural and artificial intelligence, respectively.
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citation to Kant (1781).

claim: Schemata were later adapted by psychology as a means to formalize mechanisms enabling intelligence.
source: First introduced to philosophy to explain how prior knowledge enables perception of the world (Kant, 1781), schemata were later adapted by psychology (Barlett, 1932; Piaget, 1926) and computer science (Minsky, 1975; Rumelhart, 1980) as a means to formalize mechanisms enabling natural and artificial intelligence, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to Barlett (1932) and Piaget (1926).

claim: Scene schemata represent knowledge about the typical composition of real-world environments.
source: In the narrower context of natural vision, scene schemata represent knowledge about the typical composition of real-world environments (Mandler, 1984).
evidence: This is a definitional claim supported by citation to Mandler (1984).

claim: Scene schemata entail knowledge about the distribution of objects across scenes.
source: Scene schemata for example entail knowledge about the distribution of objects across scenes, where objects appear in particular locations across the scene and in particular locations with respect to other objects (Kaiser et al., 2019a; Torralba et al., 2006; Võ et al., 2019; Wolfe et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Memory performance is boosted when scenes are configured in accordance with the schema.
source: The beneficial role of such scene schemata was first investigated in empirical studies of human memory, where memory performance is boosted when scenes are configured in accordance with the schema (Brewer and Treyens, 1981; Mandler and Johnson, 1976; Mandler and Parker, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical memory studies.

claim: Scene schemata not only organize memory contents, but also the contents of perception.
source: Recently however, it has become clear that scene schemata not only organize memory contents, but also the contents of perception.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by subsequent citations to perceptual studies.

claim: Knowledge about the structure of the world can be used to generate predictions about a scene's content.
source: For example, knowledge about the structure of the world can be used to generate predictions about a scene's content (Bar, 2009; Henderson, 2017), or to efficiently organize the concurrent representation of multiple scene elements (Kaiser et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bar (2009) and Henderson (2017).

claim: Schema-congruent naturalistic stimuli have a beneficial role across a variety of perceptual tasks, such as visual detection.
source: This position is reinforced by behavioral studies demonstrating a beneficial role of schema-congruent naturalistic stimuli across a variety of perceptual tasks, such as visual detection (Biederman et al., 1982; Davenport and Potter, 2004; Stein et al., 2015) and visual search (Kaiser et al., 2014; Torralba et al., 2006; Võ et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies on visual detection.

claim: Schema-congruent naturalistic stimuli have a beneficial role in visual search.
source: This position is reinforced by behavioral studies demonstrating a beneficial role of schema-congruent naturalistic stimuli across a variety of perceptual tasks, such as visual detection (Biederman et al., 1982; Davenport and Potter, 2004; Stein et al., 2015) and visual search (Kaiser et al., 2014; Torralba et al., 2006; Võ et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies on visual search.

claim: Scene schemata support the contextualization of fragmented sensory inputs.
source: Here, we put forward a novel function of scene schemata in visual processing: they support the contextualization of fragmented sensory inputs.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, tested through fMRI and EEG experiments.

claim: If sensory inputs are processed in relation to the schema context, scene fragments from similar typical positions should be processed similarly.
source: If sensory inputs are indeed processed in relation to the schema context, scene fragments stemming from similar typical positions within the scene should be processed similarly and fragments stemming from different positions should be processed differently.
evidence: This is a logical prediction from the hypothesis, tested in the experiments.

claim: Perceptual scene analysis can be spatiotemporally pinpointed to scene-selective cortex.
source: First, we hypothesized that this sorting occurs during perceptual scene analysis, which can be spatiotemporally pinpointed to scene-selective cortex (Baldassano et al., 2016; Epstein, 2014) and the first 250 ms of processing (Cichy et al., 2017; Harel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: Perceptual scene analysis occurs within the first 250 ms of processing.
source: First, we hypothesized that this sorting occurs during perceptual scene analysis, which can be spatiotemporally pinpointed to scene-selective cortex (Baldassano et al., 2016; Epstein, 2014) and the first 250 ms of processing (Cichy et al., 2017; Harel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior EEG/MEG studies.

claim: Schema-related effects in behavioral studies are more robustly observed along the vertical dimension.
source: Second, given that schema-related effects in behavioral studies (Mandler and Parker, 1976) are more robustly observed along the vertical dimension, where the scene structure is more rigid (i.e., the sky is almost always above the ground), we hypothesized that the cortical sorting of information should primarily occur along the vertical dimension.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mandler and Parker (1976) and general knowledge about scene structure.

claim: The sky is almost always above the ground in natural scenes.
source: Second, given that schema-related effects in behavioral studies (Mandler and Parker, 1976) are more robustly observed along the vertical dimension, where the scene structure is more rigid (i.e., the sky is almost always above the ground), we hypothesized that the cortical sorting of information should primarily occur along the vertical dimension.
evidence: This is common knowledge about natural scene structure.

claim: The stimulus set consisted of six natural scene images (three indoor, three outdoor).
source: Six natural scene images (Figure 1a) were each split into six equally-sized fragments (three vertical × 2 horizontal), resulting in 36 conditions (six scenes × 6 fragments).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli, shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Each scene was split into six equally-sized fragments (three vertical × 2 horizontal).
source: Six natural scene images (Figure 1a) were each split into six equally-sized fragments (three vertical × 2 horizontal), resulting in 36 conditions (six scenes × 6 fragments).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Thirty participants completed the fMRI experiment.
source: In separate fMRI (n = 30) and EEG (n = 20) experiments, participants viewed these fragments at central fixation while performing an indoor/outdoor categorization task to ensure engagement with the stimulus (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a description of the sample size for the fMRI experiment.

claim: Twenty participants completed the EEG experiment.
source: In separate fMRI (n = 30) and EEG (n = 20) experiments, participants viewed these fragments at central fixation while performing an indoor/outdoor categorization task to ensure engagement with the stimulus (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a description of the sample size for the EEG experiment.

claim: Participants viewed scene fragments at central fixation while performing an indoor/outdoor categorization task.
source: In separate fMRI (n = 30) and EEG (n = 20) experiments, participants viewed these fragments at central fixation while performing an indoor/outdoor categorization task to ensure engagement with the stimulus (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task, illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: All fragments were presented at central fixation, removing explicit location information.
source: Critically, this design allowed us to investigate whether the brain sorts the fragments with respect to their place in the schema in the absence of explicit location differences (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a key design feature of the experiment, illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: The fragments' vertical location predicted neural representations in OPA (t[29] = 4.12, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05).
source: The key observation was that the fragments' vertical location predicted neural representations in OPA (t[29] = 4.12, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05), but not in V1 and PPA (test statistics for all analyses and ROIs are reported in Supplementary file 1) (Figure 2d)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The fragments' vertical location did not predict neural representations in V1 and PPA.
source: The key observation was that the fragments' vertical location predicted neural representations in OPA (t[29] = 4.12, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05), but not in V1 and PPA (test statistics for all analyses and ROIs are reported in Supplementary file 1) (Figure 2d)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Vertical location predicted EEG responses between 55 ms and 685 ms (peak: t[19] = 9.03, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05).
source: The key observation was that the fragments' vertical location predicted neural representations in OPA (t[29] = 4.12, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05), but not in V1 and PPA (test statistics for all analyses and ROIs are reported in Supplementary file 1) (Figure 2d) and between 55 ms and 685 ms (peak: t[19] = 9.03, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EEG data analysis, shown in Figure 2e.

claim: No effects were observed for horizontal location.
source: No effects were observed for horizontal location, consistent with more rigid spatial scene structure in the vertical dimension (Mandler and Parker, 1976).
evidence: This is a negative finding from both fMRI and EEG analyses.

claim: The absence of horizontal location effects is consistent with more rigid spatial scene structure in the vertical dimension.
source: No effects were observed for horizontal location, consistent with more rigid spatial scene structure in the vertical dimension (Mandler and Parker, 1976).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative finding, supported by citation to Mandler and Parker (1976).

claim: Scene category was accurately predicted in OPA (t[29] = 3.12, p=0.002, pcorr <0.05).
source: In line with previous findings (Lowe et al., 2018; Walther et al., 2009), category was accurately predicted in OPA (t[29] = 3.12, p=0.002, pcorr <0.05) and PPA (t[29] = 4.26, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 2d)
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Scene category was accurately predicted in PPA (t[29] = 4.26, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05).
source: In line with previous findings (Lowe et al., 2018; Walther et al., 2009), category was accurately predicted in OPA (t[29] = 3.12, p=0.002, pcorr <0.05) and PPA (t[29] = 4.26, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 2d)
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Category predicted EEG responses from 60 ms to 775 ms (peak: t[19] = 6.39, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05).
source: In line with previous findings (Lowe et al., 2018; Walther et al., 2009), category was accurately predicted in OPA (t[29] = 3.12, p=0.002, pcorr <0.05) and PPA (t[29] = 4.26, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 2d), and from 60 ms to 775 ms (peak: t[19] = 6.39, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG data analysis, shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The absence of vertical location effects in V1 highlights that schematic coding is not tied to the analysis of simple visual features.
source: The absence of vertical location effects in V1 indeed highlights that schematic coding is not tied to the analysis of simple visual features.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative finding in V1.

claim: Removing DNN features abolished category information in fMRI signals.
source: After removing DNN features, category information was rendered non-significant in both fMRI and EEG signals.
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis removing DNN features, shown in Figure 3b/c.

claim: Removing DNN features abolished category information in EEG signals.
source: After removing DNN features, category information was rendered non-significant in both fMRI and EEG signals.
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis removing DNN features, shown in Figure 3b/c.

claim: After removing DNN features, vertical location still accounted for the neural organization in OPA (t[29] = 2.37, p = 0.012, pcorr <0.05).
source: Despite the suitability of our DNN model for modelling categorical brain responses, vertical location still accounted for the neural organization in OPA (t[29] = 2.37, p = 0.012, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 3b)
evidence: This is a key finding showing that schematic coding persists after controlling for DNN features.

claim: After removing DNN features, vertical location predicted EEG responses between 75 ms and 335 ms (peak: t[19] = 5.06, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05).
source: Despite the suitability of our DNN model for modelling categorical brain responses, vertical location still accounted for the neural organization in OPA (t[29] = 2.37, p = 0.012, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 3b) and between 75 ms and 335 ms (peak: t[19] = 5.06, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a key finding showing that schematic coding persists after controlling for DNN features.

claim: Schematic coding cannot be explained by categorization-related features extracted by DNN models.
source: This result suggests that schematic coding cannot be explained by categorization-related features extracted by DNN models.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that vertical location effects persist after removing DNN features.

claim: Vertical location predicted cortical organization in OPA when restricted to comparisons between indoor and outdoor scenes (t[29] = 3.05, p = 0.002, pcorr <0.05).
source: Vertical location still predicted cortical organization in OPA (t[29] = 3.05, p = 0.002, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 3e)
evidence: This finding demonstrates generalization across scene types.

claim: Vertical location predicted EEG responses from 70 ms to 385 ms when restricted to comparisons between indoor and outdoor scenes (peak: t[19] = 7.47, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05).
source: Vertical location still predicted cortical organization in OPA (t[29] = 3.05, p = 0.002, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 3e) and from 70 ms to 385 ms (peak: t[19] = 7.47, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 3f).
evidence: This finding demonstrates generalization across scene types.

claim: The generalization across indoor and outdoor scenes indicates that schematic coding operates similarly across radically different scenes.
source: The generalization across indoor and outdoor scenes indicates that schematic coding operates similarly across radically different scenes, suggesting that the mechanism can similarly contextualize information across different real-life situations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-category generalization finding.

claim: After removing both DNN features and within-category comparisons, OPA representations were still explained by the fragments' vertical location (t[29] = 2.38, p = 0.012, pcorr <0.05).
source: In this analysis, OPA representations were still explained by the fragments' vertical location (t[29] = 2.38, p = 0.012, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is a finding from the most stringent control analysis.

claim: After removing both DNN features and within-category comparisons, vertical location predicted EEG responses after 180 ms (peak: t[19] = 4.41, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05).
source: Notably, early schema effects were rendered non-significant, while vertical location still predicted representations after 180 ms (peak: t[19] = 4.41, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 3i), suggesting a high degree of flexibility emerging at that time.
evidence: This is a finding from the most stringent control analysis.

claim: A high degree of flexibility in schematic coding emerges after 180 ms.
source: Notably, early schema effects were rendered non-significant, while vertical location still predicted representations after 180 ms (peak: t[19] = 4.41, p<0.001, pcorr <0.05) (Figure 3i), suggesting a high degree of flexibility emerging at that time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal pattern in the most stringent control analysis.

claim: Vertical location information was exclusively found in OPA across all analyses.
source: Interestingly, across all analyses, vertical location information was exclusively found in OPA and always peaked shortly after 200 ms (see Supplementary file 2), suggesting that schematic coding occurs during early perceptual analysis of scenes.
evidence: This is a summary of the consistent pattern across all fMRI analyses.

claim: Vertical location information always peaked shortly after 200 ms across all analyses.
source: Interestingly, across all analyses, vertical location information was exclusively found in OPA and always peaked shortly after 200 ms (see Supplementary file 2), suggesting that schematic coding occurs during early perceptual analysis of scenes.
evidence: This is a summary of the consistent temporal pattern across all EEG analyses.

claim: Schematic coding occurs during early perceptual analysis of scenes.
source: Interestingly, across all analyses, vertical location information was exclusively found in OPA and always peaked shortly after 200 ms (see Supplementary file 2), suggesting that schematic coding occurs during early perceptual analysis of scenes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the consistent spatiotemporal pattern across analyses.

claim: The findings characterize a novel neural mechanism for contextualizing fragmented inputs during naturalistic vision.
source: Together, our findings characterize a novel neural mechanism for contextualizing fragmented inputs during naturalistic vision.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the main contribution of the study.

claim: The mechanism exploits schemata to sort sensory inputs into meaningful representations of the environment.
source: The mechanism exploits schemata to sort sensory inputs into meaningful representations of the environment.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Schema-based coding operates flexibly across changes in visual properties.
source: This sorting occurs during perceptual scene analysis in scene-selective OPA and within the first 200 ms of vision, and operates flexibly across changes in visual properties.
evidence: This is supported by the analyses controlling for DNN features and scene type.

claim: Schema-based coding in OPA is consistent with the region's important role in visual scene processing.
source: That schema-based coding can be localized to OPA is consistent with the region's important role in visual scene processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the findings to prior knowledge about OPA.

claim: Transcranial magnetic stimulation studies suggest that OPA activation is crucial for scene discrimination.
source: Transcranial magnetic stimulation studies suggest that OPA activation is crucial for various scene perception tasks, such as scene discrimination (Dilks et al., 2013; Ganaden et al., 2013), navigating through scenes (Julian et al., 2016) and anticipating upcoming scene information (Gandolfo and Downing, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to TMS studies.

claim: OPA activation is crucial for navigating through scenes.
source: Transcranial magnetic stimulation studies suggest that OPA activation is crucial for various scene perception tasks, such as scene discrimination (Dilks et al., 2013; Ganaden et al., 2013), navigating through scenes (Julian et al., 2016) and anticipating upcoming scene information (Gandolfo and Downing, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Julian et al. (2016).

claim: OPA activation is crucial for anticipating upcoming scene information.
source: Transcranial magnetic stimulation studies suggest that OPA activation is crucial for various scene perception tasks, such as scene discrimination (Dilks et al., 2013; Ganaden et al., 2013), navigating through scenes (Julian et al., 2016) and anticipating upcoming scene information (Gandolfo and Downing, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gandolfo and Downing (2019).

claim: Computations in the OPA include the analysis of spatial scene layout.
source: Functional MRI work suggest that computations in the OPA include the analysis of spatial scene layout (Dillon et al., 2018; Henriksson et al., 2019; Lowe et al., 2017) and the parsing of local scene elements like objects and local surfaces (Kamps et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: Computations in the OPA include the parsing of local scene elements like objects and local surfaces.
source: Functional MRI work suggest that computations in the OPA include the analysis of spatial scene layout (Dillon et al., 2018; Henriksson et al., 2019; Lowe et al., 2017) and the parsing of local scene elements like objects and local surfaces (Kamps et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kamps et al. (2016).

claim: The current study is limited to a small set of scenes.
source: As the current study is limited to a small set of scenes, more research is needed to explore whether schema-based coding generalizes to more diverse contents.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: Schema-based coding may constitute a more general coding strategy that may generalize to other visual contents (such as faces).
source: It is conceivable that schema-based coding constitutes a more general coding strategy that may generalize to other visual contents (such as faces; Henriksson et al., 2015) and non-visual processing domains: when sensory information is fragmented and spatial information is unreliable, the brain may use schematic information to contextualize sensory inputs.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential generalization, with citation to Henriksson et al. (2015).

claim: When sensory information is fragmented and spatial information is unreliable, the brain may use schematic information to contextualize sensory inputs.
source: It is conceivable that schema-based coding constitutes a more general coding strategy that may generalize to other visual contents (such as faces; Henriksson et al., 2015) and non-visual processing domains: when sensory information is fragmented and spatial information is unreliable, the brain may use schematic information to contextualize sensory inputs.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the general principle.

claim: This view is in line with Bayesian theories of perception where the importance of prior information for perceptual inference grows with the noisiness and ambiguity of the sensory information at hand.
source: This view is in line with Bayesian theories of perception where the importance of prior information for perceptual inference grows with the noisiness and ambiguity of the sensory information at hand (Ernst and Banks, 2002; Kersten et al., 2004).
evidence: This connects the findings to Bayesian theories, supported by citations.

claim: The schema-based sorting of scene representations provides a mechanism for efficient communication between perceptual and cognitive systems.
source: The schema-based sorting of scene representations provides a mechanism for efficient communication between perceptual and cognitive systems: when scene information is formatted with respect to its role in the environment, it can be efficiently read out by downstream processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: When scene information is formatted with respect to its role in the environment, it can be efficiently read out by downstream processes.
source: The schema-based sorting of scene representations provides a mechanism for efficient communication between perceptual and cognitive systems: when scene information is formatted with respect to its role in the environment, it can be efficiently read out by downstream processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Cortical representations depend on functional interactions with the environment.
source: This idea is consistent with the emerging view that cortical representations depend on functional interactions with the environment (Bonner and Epstein, 2017; Groen et al., 2018; Malcolm et al., 2016; Peelen and Downing, 2017).
evidence: This connects the findings to an emerging theoretical view, supported by citations.

claim: Formatting perceptual information according to real-world structure may allow cognitive and motor systems to efficiently read out visual information that is needed for different real-world tasks.
source: Under this view, formatting perceptual information according to real-world structure may allow cognitive and motor systems to efficiently read out visual information that is needed for different real-world tasks (e.g., immediate action versus future navigation).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the functional significance.

claim: The schema-based sorting of scene information happens already during early scene analysis.
source: As the schema-based sorting of scene information happens already during early scene analysis, many high-level processes have access to this information.
evidence: This is based on the temporal findings from the EEG data.

claim: DNNs trained on categorization accurately capture the representational divide into different scene categories.
source: While DNNs trained on categorization accurately capture the representational divide into different scene categories, they cannot explain the schema-based organization observed in the human visual system.
evidence: This is based on the finding that DNN features explain category but not vertical location information.

claim: DNNs trained on categorization cannot explain the schema-based organization observed in the human visual system.
source: While DNNs trained on categorization accurately capture the representational divide into different scene categories, they cannot explain the schema-based organization observed in the human visual system.
evidence: This is based on the finding that vertical location effects persist after removing DNN features.

claim: Current DNN models of categorization do not use real-world structure in similar ways as the human brain.
source: Although this does not mean that visual features extracted by DNN models in principle are incapable of explaining schema-based brain representations, our results highlight that current DNN models of categorization do not use real-world structure in similar ways as the human brain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications for computational modeling.

claim: Augmenting DNN training procedures with schematic information may improve their performance on real-world tasks.
source: In the future, augmenting DNN training procedures with schematic information (Katti et al., 2019) may improve their performance on real-world tasks and narrow the gap between artificial and biological neural networks.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future directions, with citation to Katti et al. (2019).

claim: By rapidly organizing visual information according to its typical role in the world, this mechanism may contribute to the optimal use of perceptual information for guiding efficient real-world behaviors.
source: By rapidly organizing visual information according to its typical role in the world, this mechanism may contribute to the optimal use of perceptual information for guiding efficient real-world behaviors, even when sensory inputs are incomplete or dynamically changing.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Participants performed very well in the indoor/outdoor categorization task (fMRI: 94% correct, 658 ms mean response time, EEG: 96%, 606 ms).
source: In both experiments, participants performed very well in the indoor/outdoor categorization task (fMRI: 94% correct, 658 ms mean response time, EEG: 96%, 606 ms).
evidence: This is a description of behavioral performance in the task.

claim: Differences in task difficulty across fragments were not related to the neural effects of interest.
source: Differences in task difficulty across fragments were not related to the neural effects of interest (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a control analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: A multi-dimensional scaling of the fragments' neural similarity in OPA revealed a sorting according to vertical location.
source: A multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) of the fragments' neural similarity in OPA (a) and after 200 ms of processing (b) revealed a sorting according to vertical location, which was visible in a two-dimensional solution.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A multi-dimensional scaling of the fragments' neural similarity after 200 ms of processing revealed a sorting according to vertical location.
source: A multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) of the fragments' neural similarity in OPA (a) and after 200 ms of processing (b) revealed a sorting according to vertical location, which was visible in a two-dimensional solution.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Schemata are a prominent organizing principle for representations in OPA and after 200 ms of vision.
source: This visualization suggests that schemata are a prominent organizing principle for representations in OPA and after 200 ms of vision.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MDS visualization in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Around 200 ms, a division into the three vertical locations can be observed in the MDS analysis.
source: Notably, around 200 ms, a division into the three vertical locations can be observed.
evidence: This is a description of Video 1 showing time-resolved MDS.

claim: The vertical location organization in the neural data reflects prior schematic knowledge about scene structure.
source: We interpret the vertical location organization in the neural data as reflecting prior schematic knowledge about scene structure.
evidence: This is the main interpretation of the vertical location effects, discussed in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The vertical location organization cannot solely be explained by extensive learning over the course of the experiment.
source: Together, these results suggest that the vertical location organization cannot solely be explained by extensive learning over the course of the experiment.
evidence: This is based on the analysis splitting data into first and second halves, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Schematic coding can be observed consistently across the different comparisons along the vertical axis.
source: Together, these results suggest that schematic coding can be observed consistently across the different comparisons along the vertical axis, although comparisons including the top fragments yielded stronger effects.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of pairwise comparisons along the vertical axis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Comparisons including the top fragments yielded stronger schematic coding effects.
source: Together, these results suggest that schematic coding can be observed consistently across the different comparisons along the vertical axis, although comparisons including the top fragments yielded stronger effects.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of pairwise comparisons along the vertical axis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The effects of schematic coding emerging around 200 ms cannot be explained by differences in task difficulty.
source: This shows that the effects of schematic coding – emerging around 200 ms after onset – cannot be explained by differences in task difficulty.
evidence: This is based on the control analysis for task difficulty, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The categorical predictor revealed significantly stronger vertical location information from 75 ms to 340 ms compared to the Euclidean predictor.
source: However, the categorical predictor revealed significantly stronger vertical location information from 75 ms to 340 ms, suggesting that, at least in the EEG data, the differentiation along the vertical axis is more categorical in nature.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of categorical versus Euclidean predictors, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9.

claim: The differentiation along the vertical axis is more categorical in nature.
source: However, the categorical predictor revealed significantly stronger vertical location information from 75 ms to 340 ms, suggesting that, at least in the EEG data, the differentiation along the vertical axis is more categorical in nature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between categorical and Euclidean predictors.

claim: Removing AlexNet DNN features rendered category information non-significant in fMRI and EEG signals.
source: Removing the AlexNet DNN features rendered category information non-significant in fMRI and EEG signals.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: After removing AlexNet DNN features, vertical location information was still found in OPA and from 65 ms to 375 ms.
source: However, we still found vertical location information in OPA and from 65 ms to 375 ms.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The results obtained with the AlexNet model are highly similar to the results obtained with the ResNet50 model.
source: In sum, these results are highly similar to the results obtained with the ResNet50 model (Figure 3b/c/h/i).
evidence: This is a comparison of results from two different DNN architectures.

claim: GLMs based on the ResNet50 RDMs had better fit than those based on AlexNet RDMs.
